topic: Course Overview, What is Calculus & Functions
core_points: Calculus derives from the Latin word for pebble (ancient computational token).
Calculus analyzes dynamic change and motion, in contrast to static algebra ($d = vt$).
The real line is continuous without gaps from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$.
A function is a deterministic relation $y = f(x)$ where every input has exactly one output.

pillars.name: Differential Calculus
pillars.desc: Splitting quantities into infinitesimal increments to determine instantaneous rates of change.

pillars.name: Integral Calculus
pillars.desc: Accumulating continuous sums of infinitesimal slices to calculate total area, volume, and length.

practice_problems: Review real line intervals, domain, and range.
common_mistakes: Confusing the function definition $f(x)$ with multiplication $f \cdot x$.
Failing the Vertical Line Test: a circle $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ is not a single function of $x$.

deep_dive.content: Elementary geometry computes areas of static polygons and constant velocities via $d = vt$. Calculus introduces the mathematics of change by approximating non-linear, dynamic curves with linear tangents through limit processes.

A function $f: D \to Y$ assigns to each element $x \in D$ exactly one element $f(x) \in Y$. Graphically, this uniqueness condition is verified by the Vertical Line Test: no vertical line $x = a$ may intersect the curve at more than one coordinate point.

topic: Real Numbers, Intervals, Absolute Value & Inequalities
core_points: Number hierarchy: $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$ along the unbroken real continuum.
Three Core Properties of $\mathbb{R}$: Algebraic Field Axioms, Order Axioms, and the Completeness Axiom.
Intervals (Finite vs. Infinite): Open $(a, b)$, closed $[a, b]$, and half-open $[a, b)$ subsets.
Absolute Value: Geometrically, $|x - c|$ represents distance; algebraically defined as $x$ if $x \ge 0$, and $-x$ if $x < 0$.
Inequality Transversals: $a < b \implies a + c < b + c$, but $c < 0 \implies ac > bc$ (sign reversal).
common_mistakes: Multiplying an inequality by an algebraic variable without testing whether that variable is positive or negative.
Writing disjoint intervals with 'and' instead of set union notation: $(-\infty, -2) \cup (2, \infty)$.
Treating $\sqrt{x^2}$ as simply $x$ instead of the mathematically rigorous $|x|$.

deep_dive.content: While rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ are dense on the line, $\mathbb{Q}$ contains infinitely many holes (e.g., $\sqrt{2}$, $\pi$, $e$). The Completeness Axiom guarantees that the real line $\mathbb{R}$ has zero gaps: every non-empty subset $S \subset \mathbb{R}$ bounded above possesses a least upper bound (supremum) in $\mathbb{R}$. Calculus limits depend directly on this unbroken continuum.

Algebraically, $|x|$ is defined piecewise. Geometrically, $|a - b|$ measures the Euclidean 1D distance between $a$ and $b$. Solving $|x - c| < \delta$ defines an open symmetric neighborhood $(c - \delta, c + \delta)$ centered at $c$ with radius $\delta$—the exact structural foundation for the formal $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ definition of limits.

Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative constant reverses the inequality sign: $a < b \iff -a > -b$. Geometrically, multiplying by a negative scalar reflects points across the origin ($0$), inverting their directional order along the coordinate axis.
